title: Vishvamitra and the forbidden food
hook: in a famine, a great sage creeps into a hut at night to steal a piece of dog meat, and gets caught
carry: apaddharma: dharma bends to save a life
tomorrow: a hunter shelters under a pigeon's tree. what is a guest owed?

segments.voice: Yesterday Bhishma said a king stands between the big fish and the small. Your line was rajadharma, power is for protecting the small.

Yudhishthira asks a hard question. What happens to dharma when everything falls apart? When there's war, famine, collapse, and the normal rules can't be kept? Bhishma's answer is a whole section called Apaddharma, dharma in times of distress. To explain it, he tells a story that's uncomfortable on purpose. A great sage, Vishvamitra, is starving. The rains have failed for a long time. The fields are dust, the villages empty, and people eat whatever they can find. One night, half dead, Vishvamitra slips into a poor hamlet looking for food.
screen: `WHEN THE RULES RUN OUT.` → `APADDHARMA.` → `A STARVING SAGE AT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: In one hut he sees the haunch of a dog hanging. By the rules of his world, it's deeply forbidden food for a man like him. He decides to take it anyway. But the man who lives there wakes and catches him, and what follows isn't a fight. It's a debate. The householder, a man the society of that time placed at the bottom, argues for the rules. You're a sage, he says. You know dharma. Don't do this. Vishvamitra argues back. Staying alive comes first, because only the living can practice dharma at all. When I'm through this, I'll make amends with austerity. A dead sage helps no one. The householder isn't fully convinced, but Vishvamitra takes the meat, and even now, the story says, he means to offer it to the gods before he eats. Then the god Indra sends rain. The great sage steals; the man at the bottom defends dharma; the story leaves the discomfort in place. Two Hindu teachings sit inside it. Apaddharma: in real distress, dharma bends to protect life. And prayashchitta: the amends you make afterward, which is why Vishvamitra speaks of austerity even with the meat in his hand. But Bhishma warns this is for real distress, not convenience. A king who calls every inconvenience a famine has missed the lesson. You can still see this in Hindu homes. Many teachers say the sick and the very old may eat on a fast day, or keep a lighter fast with fruit or milk. The fast serves life. It was never meant to cost one.
screen: `THE FORBIDDEN FOOD` · `THE HOUSEHOLDER ARGUES FOR THE RULES` · `"ONLY THE LIVING PRACTICE DHARMA"` · then, large: `DHARMA BENDS TO SAVE A LIFE`

segments.voice: Let your breath settle and bring to mind a time you bent one of your own rules because things were falling apart. Breathe in and remember what was at stake; breathe out and ask honestly, without judging yourself, whether it was a real emergency or just convenience, and whether anything still needs repairing. If you pray, you can bring it into your prayer.
Apaddharma. Dharma for times of distress: a starving sage who stole forbidden food, and the man who argued with him.
Your line: apaddharma, dharma bends to save a life. Tomorrow, a pair of pigeons and a hunter. See you then.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers and writers on dharma discuss Apaddharma, the conduct allowed in real distress, and the story of Vishvamitra and the dog meat is told as a hard example of it.

fork.setup: a friend says: 'if dharma can bend in a famine, i can skip my promises whenever i'm busy.' by Bhishma's teaching, what's the answer?
options: no: it bends only in real distress, to protect life, and you make amends after.
no: dharma never bends, not even in a famine.
fork.reveal: apaddharma is for real distress, not convenience, and it comes with prayashchitta, the amends afterward. busy isn't a famine.

original.note: dharma in distress: conduct for times when the ordinary rules can't be kept.

trapdoor: what you thought: dharma means never breaking the rules.
what it means: apaddharma: in real distress a rule may bend to save life, with amends (prayashchitta) after.
what a scholar hears: the story deliberately reverses rank, with the sage stealing and the man at the bottom defending dharma, so the reader can't settle the question easily.
